urls.description: From the Great Recession until 2019, U.S. labor productivity growth disappointed. Nonfarm-business output per hour grew about 1 percent a year from 2010 to 2019, down from 3 percent in the late 1990s. This slowdown was especially pronounced in manufacturing, and it coincided with a slowdown in the growth of revenue per worker among public firms. However, since 2019, growth has picked up to twice the 2010s rate, around 2 percent. In this post, I use data from firms’ 10-K filings to unpack this recent acceleration. I first show that the acceleration appears in public firms’ revenue per worker, then document how the gains went into profit margins, and finally, what firm characteristics predicted significant profit margin increases. The increase in profit margins is consistent with ongoing declines in the labor share of output.
urls.title: Revenue per Worker Is Up. Are Firms Getting a Larger Share? - Liberty Street Economics

Two competing forces—geopolitical developments and the AI-driven technology cycle —are reshaping the global economy. Together with profoud demographic and trade shifts and persistent imbalances, these crosscurrents are reconfiguring the global landscape and raising important questions about the path ahead. As policymakers navigate near-term disruptions, they must also lay the foundations for stronger, balanced and inclusive medium-term growth. Against this backdrop, this debate will explore how countries can build resilient and dynamic economies in an increasingly fragmented and uneven global landscape. Daly (Reuters, post-CPI): “More likely than not to need additional adjustments,” but no rush: “Why force urgency when you don’t need to have urgency?… We have more meetings ahead of us.”

Ok so this book WAS very fun. Big picture takeaways:

- universities have always had an unstable business model, which is constantly evolving. The current bundle of education and research need not last forever either.

- all the culture war stuff we're debating now has been there for literally 800 years. Students have always partied and had sex and wanted to overthrow authority and cross dress and haze each other, and parents and governments have always attempted to exert control, and the relative power of each has oscillated. Colleges used to have their own jails! U of Uppsala executed a student via DEATH PENALTY as late as 1770s!

- the health of the industry has oscillated a ton, with European enrollments dropping by as much as half in certain decades and centuries.

- realistically, the best way to protect universities from being defunded is for all professors to work at least partially on weapons systems

- the book (and others on this topic) has made it increasingly annoying to listen to non-historian analysts comment on the academic industry, because seemingly none of them seem to be aware that basically none of the phenomena they are analyzing are new.

The book is not perfect. It's ostensibly a history told via architecture, but that connection is meh. And there's not an attempt to give a proper socio-economic analysis of the evolution of universities, it reads more as a collection of facts.

But the facts are awesome, so I highly recommend!
